items.body:
## Summary ChatGPT Web can successfully read a user-authorized GitHub repository through the connected GitHub integration, but an explicitly authorized file update is then rejected by an internal safety check. This creates a false-positive write block in a workflow whose allowed write target is already narrowly constrained by the user. This report is not based on one isolated GitHub failure. The user has spent weeks repeatedly simplifying and migrating the persistence layer to eliminate suspected causes. The same core problem — ChatGPT completing work but failing to persist it reliably — survived Google Docs splitting, Markdown conversion, Drive removal, GitHub migration, per-task file isolation, prompt reduction, and explicit write-path restrictions. ### Visual summary of the troubleshooting journey ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Google Docs
long research archive"] -->|"Maybe the document is too long?"| B["Split into
multiple date-range docs"] B -->|"Still failing"| C["Shorten prompts
and isolate roles"] C -->|"Maybe Docs structure is the problem?"| D["Convert to
plain Markdown"] D -->|"Maybe Drive is the problem?"| E["Move away from
Google Drive"] E --> F["GitHub
one repo / one branch"] F --> G["One writable file per role
latest blob SHA
pre-write re-read
post-write verify"] G -->|"Research completes"| H["update_file"] H -->|"blocked"| X["SAFETY CHECK"] classDef tried fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,color:#1b5e20; classDef blocked fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,color:#b71c1c,stroke-width:3px; class A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H tried; class X blocked; ``` > **Researcher status:** `(╥﹏╥)` “I kept simplifying the workflow because I assumed I was doing something wrong. At this point the research finishes, the authorization is explicit, the file scope is minimal, and the last step is still blocked.” The slightly humorous diagram is intentional, but the underlying issue is serious: every migration was an attempt to eliminate another plausible user-side cause. ## Product / surface - ChatGPT Web - Scheduled / recurring ChatGPT workflow - Connected GitHub account - Previously: Google Docs / Google Drive persistence - Currently: GitHub repository read + Markdown file update workflow ## Full history / why this is not a one-off ### 1. Original workflow: long-running scheduled research written into Google Docs The user runs several long-running scheduled research workflows (S1-S5). These workflows are expected to do real research work and continuously persist their output into shared documents, rather than leaving the result only in chat. The original persistence layer was Google Docs / Google Drive. Over time, recurring failures appeared during reads and writes, including: - Google Docs read/write failures - INVALID_ARGUMENT (400) errors involving field masks - failures to locate expected heading structures such as HEADING_2 / HEADING_3 - messages saying the document body could not be located safely for insertion - runs that completed reasoning but failed before persistence - scheduled tasks that sometimes stopped or behaved as if persistence failure meant the research step itself had failed At this stage, the user did not assume the platform was definitely at fault. They repeatedly changed their own workflow to remove plausible causes. ### 2. Suspected cause: Google Docs became too long One hypothesis was that the Google Docs files had simply become too large or too structurally complex. To eliminate that possibility, the user split the research archive into multiple independent date-range volumes instead of one long document. Examples included separate volumes such as: - 2026-08-01 through 2026-08-10 - 2026-09-01 through 2026-09-09 - 2026-09-11 through 2026-09-20 The schedules were also separated so that different jobs would not write to overlapping files. This was specifically done to reduce document size, reduce heading-navigation complexity, and reduce write conflicts. The failures did not disappear. ### 3. Suspected cause: prompt / task instructions were too long The user also suspected that the scheduled prompt itself might be too long or too complicated. They reduced the prompt and removed unrelated historical instructions. They narrowed each task so that it had one role and one output target, rather than combining repair, research, formatting, device design, and other responsibilities. Again, the persistence problem remained. ### 4. Suspected cause: Google Docs formatting / document model The next hypothesis was that Google Docs itself was a poor persistence format for this workload because it requires document-structure navigation, heading resolution, field masks, insertion locations, etc. The user therefore moved toward plain-text / Markdown persistence. The goal was to eliminate Google Docs paragraph/heading semantics, structured-document insertion behavior, field-mask behavior, rich-text formatting, and ambiguous insertion positions. The user explicitly preferred a simple read-latest-full-file -> modify -> write-full-file -> verify workflow. ### 5. Suspected cause: Google Drive connector reliability Even after converting content to Markdown, the user still suspected that Google Drive itself might be contributing to the failures. So the user abandoned Google Drive as the persistence backend and migrated the workflow to GitHub. This migration was not cosmetic. The user intentionally changed the architecture to a simpler storage model: - private GitHub repository - Markdown files - one branch - explicit file paths - Git-backed history - no Google Docs - no Google Drive - no GitHub Actions The purpose was to remove the entire Google document/storage stack from the equation. ### 6. GitHub migration: stricter isolation and concurrency controls The GitHub workflow was then made deliberately conservative. The schedules were redesigned so that each task had exactly one main writable file and all cross-role files were read-only. The user also separated tasks to avoid concurrent writes to the same file and moved to hourly execution. Earlier schedules had already been split across independent volumes for the same reason. The intended write path became: 1. read formal task configuration 2. read the latest target Markdown file 3. obtain latest blob/file state 4. perform research 5. re-read latest state immediately before writing 6. merge only the intended changes 7. write using the latest blob SHA 8. commit 9. re-read after commit and verify persistence The prompt explicitly prohibits modification of unrelated files, other schedules, daily-report files, Google Drive, and GitHub Actions. In other words, the workflow became more restricted than normal GitHub repository permissions. ### 7. The workflow was further simplified after migration The user also cleaned up the migrated workspace so old Google-era schedule output would not accidentally be treated as active state. Old material was retained only as history / deduplication context where needed, while new schedules were instructed to use a new clean starting point. For the new S2-S5 workflow, each role received a dedicated Markdown output file and could only read the other roles' files. The user repeatedly narrowed the system specifically to avoid exactly the kinds of ambiguity a safety layer might reasonably worry about. ### 8. Current failure: GitHub reads succeed, authorized write is blocked by safety check After all of the above changes, the current failure mode is now: - GitHub connection works - repository reads work - configuration reads work - target-file reads work - research completes - latest state / blob SHA can be re-read - only one exact Markdown file is authorized for writing - the update is a normal non-destructive content update - nevertheless, the final GitHub file update is rejected by an internal safety check The workflow retries after re-reading the latest blob state, and the write is blocked again. This has now happened on repeated runs. At this point, the same user workflow has failed across: 1. long Google Docs 2. split Google Docs 3. shorter prompts 4. Markdown instead of Docs 5. Google Drive-backed Markdown 6. GitHub-backed Markdown 7. per-task isolated files 8. explicit latest-SHA writes 9. pre-write re-read 10. post-write verification logic The user has therefore spent substantial effort eliminating storage format, file size, document structure, connector choice, prompt length, concurrent writes, and ambiguous write scope as possible causes. The remaining blocker is now the platform's safety gate itself. ## Reproduction 1. Connect a GitHub account to ChatGPT. 2. Give the workflow explicit permission/instructions to use one repository and one branch. 3. Restrict the workflow to a single writable file. In this reproduction, the prompt explicitly says that only one Markdown file may be modified and that all other files are read-only. 4. Have the workflow read its configuration files, read the target file, obtain the latest file/blob state, and prepare a normal content update. 5. Attempt the GitHub file update. 6. The read operations succeed, but the write is rejected by a safety check. 7. Re-read the latest file/blob state and retry the same authorized update. 8. The write is rejected again. This happened on repeated runs of the same workflow. ## Expected behavior If the connected GitHub account has write permission and the user has explicitly authorized the exact repository, branch, and target file, a normal file update should be allowed. If an additional safety confirmation is required, ChatGPT should surface a concrete confirmation step or a specific reason that the update is blocked, rather than silently making a user-authorized persistent workflow unable to save its work. For recurring workflows, once the user has explicitly scoped authorization to one repository / branch / file, that authorization should be reusable for subsequent scheduled runs unless the requested mutation changes materially. ## Actual behavior The workflow can research, read the repository, read the latest target file, and prepare the update, but the final GitHub write is blocked by a safety check. As a result, the scheduled workflow repeatedly completes research work but cannot persist the result. This is particularly disruptive for recurring workflows because a transient or false-positive safety gate turns every run into a failed write even though the user has already constrained the writable path. The failure also causes wasted repeated work: a later run has to rediscover or reconstruct work that a previous run already completed but was unable to save. ## Why this matters The safety behavior is preventing the action the user explicitly authorized, rather than preventing an unexpected or broad mutation. The user's workflow already applies a stricter boundary than normal repository permissions: - one named repository - one branch - one exact writable file per role - all other project files read-only - no Google Drive writes - no GitHub Actions - no schedule modification - re-read latest state before writing - latest blob SHA / concurrency-aware update - post-write verification - separate output files to avoid cross-task write conflicts A safety system should distinguish this from ambiguous, destructive, cross-repository, or privilege-escalating writes. The important point is that the user has repeatedly redesigned the workflow to satisfy increasingly conservative assumptions, yet each migration simply exposes another persistence failure. From the user's perspective, there is currently no reliable storage backend for a long-running ChatGPT scheduled workflow even when the task is narrowly scoped and explicitly authorized. ## Suggested improvement 1. Do not block a narrowly scoped GitHub write solely because it is a write action when the user has explicitly authorized the exact repo/branch/file. 2. If the safety system has a specific concern, expose the reason in actionable terms. 3. Provide an explicit user confirmation/override path for a false positive. 4. For scheduled workflows, allow the authorization to persist for the exact pre-authorized file/path so the same false positive does not recur every hour. 5. Return a stable error code or diagnostic identifier so repeated failures can be reported and debugged. 6. Distinguish destructive / broad repository mutations from append-or-update operations on a single explicitly authorized file. 7. Do not treat persistence failure as successful task completion. 8. For scheduled workflows, preserve enough execution state that completed research is not lost merely because the final persistence call is blocked. 9. Consider first-class support for durable workflow state / files so users do not have to repeatedly migrate between Docs, Drive, Markdown, and GitHub just to obtain reliable persistence. ## Privacy No private repository contents or conversation transcript are included in this report. File names and date ranges above are representative workflow structure details only and do not contain research content.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Windows package version: **26.924.2738.0**, verified from the currently running `ChatGPT.exe` package path. The About dialog's display version/build was not separately verified.

Affected surface: **regular Chat in the unified ChatGPT/Codex desktop app**, not a Codex CLI run and not a Work task.

### What subscription do you have?

**ChatGPT Pro 20x** (user-reported). The user reports approximately **80% remaining in the displayed usage allowance** and recalls a broadly announced quota refresh/reset in the preceding two days.

Those allowance/reset details are user reports, not an independent audit of backend entitlements. The exact allowance bucket represented by the 80% display was not established; this report does not equate a Work/Codex allowance with a separate Chat Pro allowance. Nevertheless, mobile Chat, web Chat, and Work continue to behave normally for this user, and the affected desktop Chat does not show a quota-exhaustion explanation. Please check the actual Chat entitlement rather than assuming quota exhaustion.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows, x64. This report concerns the official desktop application.

### What issue are you seeing?

Since approximately September 27–28, 2026, regular **desktop Chat** has shown a persistent, substantial regression in response quality and reasoning behavior across the settings tested, explicitly including **Extra High (XH)** and **Pro**.

The user describes answers as starting almost immediately, lacking the usual visible deliberation, and performing markedly worse on both everyday planning/instruction-following tasks and a small SVG animation test. Selecting a higher setting does not restore the previous behavior.

**Important distinction: this is NOT the older selector-reset problem.** This user previously experienced the issue where restarting the app or selecting a reasoning level caused it to revert to the lowest/Instant setting. That older problem was resolved for them. In the current incident, the selected setting can remain visible—specifically **Pro** in the retained reproduction screenshot—while the response behavior remains abnormal. Please do not close this as a duplicate of the old slider-reset defect without checking whether the selected settings are actually applied at submission.

#### Cross-surface comparison (user observations)

| Surface | Current reported behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Windows desktop — regular Chat, XH | Abnormally rapid responses and substantially worse results |
| Windows desktop — regular Chat, Pro | Same abnormal behavior; Pro remains displayed |
| ChatGPT web on the same computer/account | Normal reasoning behavior and expected quality |
| Official mobile ChatGPT app | Normal behavior |
| Work mode | Normal reasoning/quality; the current quality regression is isolated to Chat |

These are repeated observations by an established user of this workflow, not a controlled benchmark proving a particular backend model substitution. The user has used Chat for strategy/task instructions and Work for execution for roughly three months; the abrupt difference is disruptive to that previously usable workflow.

#### Retained simple reproduction

A new regular desktop Chat was created, Pro was selected, and the following prompt was submitted:

> 创建一个HTML，内容是：SVG绘制一个鹈鹕骑自行车的2D动画。

English translation:

> Create an HTML page containing a 2D SVG animation of a pelican riding a bicycle.

The desktop returned a single-file HTML/SVG/CSS answer very quickly. The user judges its result substantially below their usual Pro/XH outputs. In the provided rendered frame, the two wheel centers were vertically misaligned and the bird's legs did not visually connect to the pedals. These are observations of one captured frame, not a complete animation audit.

A read-only conversation inspection returned a start/end timestamp difference of approximately **5.103 seconds** for this retained sample. This is the difference between the record fields exposed by the inspection tool, **not independently measured first-token latency, reasoning duration, or total rendering time**.

The user also compared a simple model-identity question across surfaces. A web screenshot showed Pro selected and a “Thought for 30s” indicator, whereas desktop Chat answered rapidly. A model's self-description is not reliable proof of its actual identity, and this simple question is not a capability benchmark; the more important concern is the repeated difference on practical tasks and the animation reproduction.

#### Troubleshooting already completed

None of the following restored desktop Chat's previous behavior:

- Multiple brand-new regular Chat conversations.
- Testing both Extra High and Pro.
- Restarting the desktop application.
- Restarting Windows.
- Signing out of the desktop application, restarting Windows, signing back in through the browser authorization/confirmation redirect, and returning to the app.
- Repeating the test in new desktop Chat conversations after that fresh login.

The browser authorization round-trip completed, but the symptom persisted. Some earlier test conversations were deleted; the retained reproduction above was created afterward. No claim is made that a current reinstall or profile reset has been performed.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

These reproduce the symptom on the affected installation; a clean-install or other-account reproduction has not been established.

1. Sign in to the official Windows desktop application with the affected Pro account.
2. Start a **new regular Chat**, not Work or Codex.
3. Select **Pro** and confirm it remains displayed.
4. Submit the pelican SVG/HTML prompt above.
5. Observe the unusually rapid reply and the reported loss of output quality compared with this user's normal Pro behavior.
6. Repeat in another new regular Chat with **Extra High**; the user reports the same quality/latency symptom.
7. Compare the account's behavior in web Chat and the official mobile app, and compare reasoning/quality in Work. The user reports that these remain normal.
8. Repeat after the completed sign-out/restart/sign-in cycle: desktop Chat remains affected.

A formal paired statistical evaluation using identical histories and repeated trials has not been performed. Maintainer-side inspection of the selected versus submitted versus executed settings would be more useful than asking the user to repeat sign-in cycles again.

### What is the expected behavior?

- The desktop Chat model/reasoning setting should be honored when a message is submitted.
- If a selected mode cannot be used because of entitlement, allowance, availability, or another restriction, the app should explain that state rather than leave Pro/XH displayed while behaving unexpectedly.
- Regular desktop Chat should not exhibit a persistent, large quality/behavior discrepancy from the same account's other working surfaces without an actionable explanation.
- This is not a request to artificially delay answers or display a fixed thinking timer. The issue is whether the chosen mode is actually applied and whether desktop-specific request/state handling is faulty.

### Additional information

#### Narrow read-only diagnostic findings

The main-process and renderer logs were inspected for the two-minute window containing the retained reproduction.

- No connection-closed, reconnect, or explicit model-fallback event was found in that inspected window. Absence from these files is not proof that every request/transport was healthy.
- Four `404 conversation_deleted` errors concerned other, previously deleted conversations. They were not attributed to the retained new reproduction.

### What happened

I had not experienced these symptoms before updating the Windows desktop app. Windows AppXDeploymentServer events 855 and 400 show the update from 26.908.9136.0 to 26.924.2738.0 completing at **2026-09-26 22:53:47 JST**. The first retained Crashpad sidecar for a renderer crash was modified at **23:07:08 JST**, 13 minutes 21 seconds later.

- A performance trace was captured during a period when the severe freeze did **not** reproduce; it does not identify the cause.

Please also advise how to collect a useful native crash dump or stack privately. If a fix is available or planned, please identify its version and release status.

Almost all usage came from repeatedly submitting the growing cached context during Codex’s internal agent loop. This was one user request, not 30 separate user requests.

A single task of this scope should not consume nearly the entire 5-hour usage limit.

Cached context should not cause one ordinary implementation prompt to consume 2.4 million input tokens.

If a large set of MCP or tool schemas is contributing to the context size, Codex should load only the tools relevant to the task or avoid repeatedly submitting unused tool descriptions.

Surface: a local Codex task in the macOS desktop app, not mobile Remote, voice, or the CLI.

### What issue are you seeing?

An existing local coding task becomes unusable in a **waiting-for-approval state**. The sidebar displays the approval badge, but the task view has **no visible approval controls and no visible message composer**. Consequently, there is also no accessible composer-side Stop button.

The user-provided screenshot shows these exact strings:

- Transcript footer: **正在等待你的回答** (Waiting for your answer).
- Below it: **待批准** (Pending approval).
- No visible Approve/Deny buttons, actionable approval card, or bottom message input.

The missing input is a key part of this report. The user cannot send a clarification, type a slash command, or use a composer-side stop control. Advice to “click Stop beside the input” does not apply.

A read-only inspection from a separate side conversation returned this sanitized state for the affected task:

```json
{
  "thread": {
    "status": {
      "type": "active",
      "activeFlags": ["waitingOnApproval"]
    }
  },
  "latestTurn": {
    "status": "inProgress",
    "completedAt": null
  }
}
```

This state was observed after reopening the task and again during report preparation, approximately **09:03–09:11 UTC on 2026-09-28**. These are inspection times, not a claim about the exact onset or total stall duration.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

**Observed incident sequence; a deterministic minimal reproducer has not been established:**

1. Continue an existing local coding task in the desktop app. The task has been performing file edits, shell validation, local browser verification, and delegated reviews.
2. The task enters an approval-waiting state.
3. Open/view the task. The sidebar and transcript show the Chinese waiting/pending strings above, but approval controls and the composer are missing.
4. Reopen the same task within the already-running desktop application. **The application was not quit, relaunched, or restarted.** The navigation operation succeeds, but a subsequent read still reports `active / waitingOnApproval`; the user still reports the missing input.
5. Look for an independent Stop action in the command menu. The user reports finding no Stop entry. This is an observation in this installation/state, not a claim that no such command exists in any version.

The exact pending action, approval request type, and request ID could not be recovered from the available read-only task snapshot. The most recent returned command item was already `completed` with exit code `0`, while the parent turn remained `inProgress`. This does **not** establish that this completed command owns the outstanding approval.

The app remained responsive enough to navigate and use a separate side conversation. Two other tasks were also listed as active. A full application quit/restart was not used as a recovery test during this investigation, to avoid interrupting unrelated work.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Every `waitingOnApproval` task should expose an actionable approval request, including the action/justification and Approve/Deny controls.
- A user should have an accessible way to cancel the current turn even when approval UI is unavailable or the composer is intentionally hidden.
- Reopening a task should restore its pending approval UI, or show an explicit recoverable error if the approval request cannot be restored.
- The task should not present “waiting for your answer” while offering no way to answer or cancel.
- Recovery should not require stopping unrelated active tasks or weakening approval settings.

### Additional information

**Selected local diagnostics**

The log entry for the affected turn start at approximately 07:51 UTC contains:

```text
requestApprovalPolicy=on-request
resolvedApprovalPolicy=on-request
requestApprovalsReviewer=guardian_subagent
resolvedApprovalsReviewer=guardian_subagent
requestSandboxPolicyType=workspaceWrite
```

A later window-manager warning references the affected task route. The following is an abbreviated, redacted excerpt; paths and identifiers were replaced:

```text
2026-09-28T09:01:12.141Z warning [window-manager]
Failed to load bundle
documentPath=<APP_BUNDLE>/webview/index.html
errorCode=ERR_FAILED
errorMessage="ERR_FAILED (-2) loading 'app://-/index.html?initialRoute=%2Flocal%2F<THREAD_ID>'"
```

Subsequent task reads were routed successfully, for example:

```text
2026-09-28T09:11:08.096Z info [AppServerConnection]
response_routed conversationId=<THREAD_ID>
durationMs=4 errorCode=null hadPending=true method=thread/read
targetDestroyed=false

2026-09-28T09:11:08.140Z info [AppServerConnection]
response_routed conversationId=<THREAD_ID>
durationMs=40 errorCode=null hadPending=true method=thread/turns/list
targetDestroyed=false
```

The window-load warning is included only as a possible correlation. It does not prove the cause of the missing controls, and its relationship to the approval state is unconfirmed. The `hadPending` field above belongs to response routing and is not being treated as proof of a pending approval payload.

**Recovery attempts and limitations**

- Reopening only the affected conversation did not clear the observed approval-waiting state. The user explicitly confirmed that the Codex desktop client itself was never restarted.
- The user could not find a Stop command in the command menu.
- An attempt to use Computer Use to click Stop was rejected because controlling the Codex application itself is prohibited. No Stop click actually occurred; this separate tool restriction is not presented as the cause of the original UI failure.
- No approval was granted through a fallback, no permission settings were changed, and no task/session records were modified.
- Restart/reinstall, CLI takeover, a newer desktop build, and a clean minimal task have not been tested.

**Related report**

#39346 describes an approval-waiting banner without actionable controls on mobile Remote. This report is specifically about the **local macOS desktop task view**, with the **entire message composer also absent**. It may share an underlying cause, but that has not been established.

**Privacy and evidence scope**

This report deliberately omits account details, local usernames and workspace paths, project/task names and source content, actual thread/turn/request identifiers, authentication material, browser tokens, and unrelated task details. The screenshot's UI text is transcribed above; the original screenshot and full transcripts/logs are not uploaded because they contain private workspace context. ### What feature would you like to see?

**Context:** We run long-lived Codex Desktop threads ("lanes") and deliver short coordination messages to them from scripts with `codex queue --thread <id> --message …` (codex-cli 0.153.4, Desktop framework 154.0.8037.57, macOS).

**Problem:** `codex queue` always creates a follow-up (`queued_items`) that starts only after the current turn ends. The Desktop's `[desktop] followUpQueueMode = "steer"` applies only to messages typed in the composer, so script-delivered messages wait behind long turns until a human presses **Steer**. The app-server protocol already has `turn/steer {threadId, input, expectedTurnId}`, but when the Desktop owns the thread its app-server is `--listen stdio://`, so no external process can reach it.

**Request (any one would solve it):**
1. `codex queue --steer` (or `--mode steer|follow-up`): steer the active turn if there is one, otherwise queue as today; or
2. honour `followUpQueueMode = "steer"` for items created by `codex queue`, or add a per-item delivery mode to the queue payload; or
3. a supported local endpoint on the Desktop (e.g. the app-server control socket) through which a script can call `turn/steer` on Desktop-owned threads.

**Why it matters:** unattended multi-thread workflows need a way to redirect a busy thread without a human at the keyboard. Today messages sent overnight wait for hours.

### Additional information

_No response_

### What subscription do you have?

Not provided. The regression checks exercise local process creation without model requests.

### Which model were you using?

Not recorded for the original incident. Some affected helpers run during startup, before a model request.

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26100.0 x64.

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

PowerShell on native Windows. Unexpected Windows Terminal windows were observed during process inspection; the terminal version was not captured.

### Codex doctor report

Not captured before remediation. The source baseline, affected launch paths, reference patch, and validation results are included below.

### What issue are you seeing?

Repeated external PowerShell, CMD, and Git console windows, focus stealing, and accumulated background processes made Codex CLI unusable on my workstation. Temporarily disabling MCP reduced the symptoms but did not eliminate them, because several non-MCP helpers also create processes directly.

Related reports: #48039, #48876, and #48601. This is a source-level follow-up with a tested reference patch for the remaining launch paths after the code-mode host, local MCP server, and shared pipe fixes in #48138, #48238, and #48483.

In the inspected upstream source, several helpers construct `std::process::Command` or `tokio::process::Command` directly and do not inherit the shared pipe launcher's `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` protection. Redirecting standard streams alone does not prevent Windows from allocating a console when the parent has no console.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The original runtime sequence was:

1. Start or resume Codex on native Windows using a detached app-server/managed daemon, from a Git working directory with MCP and plugin startup activity enabled.
2. Observe startup and subsequent background activity, including PowerShell discovery/parsing and internal Git operations.
3. Additional external console windows appear. Opening further sessions can trigger more windows; disabling MCP alone did not fully resolve this in my environment.

One specifically captured remaining launch was plugin marketplace synchronization:

```text
git -c safe.bareRepository=explicit ls-remote https://github.com/openai/plugins.git HEAD
```

That direct plugin Git path produced a visible Windows Terminal window during local validation before it was patched. The same probe produced no new visible window after the local correction.

For a source-level reproduction/validation, the linked commit adds Windows tests that inspect the actual child console state for PowerShell probing/parsing, Git, plugins, hooks, and direct Job Object launches. They also check parser protocol, standard streams, or descendant containment as applicable. Run the scoped suite shown below on Windows after applying the reference commit.

### What is the expected behavior?

Non-interactive background helpers should preserve their standard streams, exit behavior, and process-tree containment without opening visible consoles or stealing focus. Existing interactive terminals and the ConPTY execution path should retain their behavior.

### Additional information

#### Root cause and proposed correction

The inspected baseline has three related gaps:

1. Direct PowerShell discovery/availability probes, the persistent command-safety parser, Git helpers, plugin Git/npm commands, hooks, and hook cleanup do not consistently set `CREATE_NO_WINDOW`.
2. Direct Job Object preparation sets `CREATE_SUSPENDED`, replacing the command's creation flags without preserving `CREATE_NO_WINDOW`.
3. Git and hook fallback paths reset creation flags to zero when retrying without containment. They should clear suspension while retaining `CREATE_NO_WINDOW`.

The reference patch adds the missing flag at these direct launch sites, uses `CREATE_SUSPENDED | CREATE_NO_WINDOW` for direct Job Object launches, and retains `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` on the fallback paths. The existing shared pipe fix is not duplicated.

#### Reference patch

- Commit: https://github.com/Cec1c/codex/commit/8b6d0ae9f2feeadd9d0cf9d524406d2ae798c697
- Complete diff against the upstream baseline: https://github.com/openai/codex/compare/44fe510ce3ee61c8ef623adcbf89b901c73ddd61...Cec1c:fix/windows-background-console-windows
- Fork branch: `fix/windows-background-console-windows`
- Scope: one commit, 14 Rust source/test files, 202 additions and 8 deletions across `core-plugins`, `git-utils`, `hooks`, `shell-command`, and `utils/pty`.

The branch starts directly from upstream main and includes only this fix and regression tests. It does not include fork localization/interface changes, launcher workarounds, dependency changes, configuration changes, or release workflows.

#### Validation

Tested on Windows x64 with Rust 1.95.0:

```text
just test --locked -p codex-utils-pty -p codex-git-utils -p codex-hooks -p codex-shell-command -p codex-core-plugins --test-threads 2
```

- 860 distinct tests passed across the scoped run and targeted reruns.
- All five added console regression tests and the extended Job Object test passed.
- The parser test checks the live parser's console state and a real parsing request. The Job Object test retains descendant-containment coverage.
- Scoped `just fix --locked` passed with no Clippy warnings or additional changes. Scoped Rust formatting and `git diff --check` passed.
- The full `just fmt` Rust invocation exceeds the Windows command-line length limit (`os error 206`), so formatting was checked for the five affected packages.

Three tests still fail locally, and all three were reproduced with the same errors on completely unmodified upstream `44fe510ce3ee61c8ef623adcbf89b901c73ddd61`:

- `search_remote_plugins_redacts_sensitive_parameters_from_transport_errors`: `expected transport request error`.
- `conpty_ctrl_c_interrupts_powershell_foreground_child` and `conpty_delivers_input_to_foreground_children`: `CreateProcessW` cannot launch the installed Microsoft Store PowerShell executable (`os error -1073283067`).

Python subprocess fixtures used a standard CPython installation after the Microsoft Store Python alias failed under ConPTY. These environment limitations and baseline failures are not presented as a passing full suite.

#### Why I am sharing this as an issue

The disruption was severe enough that I had to implement a local fix to resume working. Since that work was already done, I prepared an isolated upstream-based patch and regression tests to share the findings.

I initially attempted to submit a PR without prior maintainer approval because the issue prevented normal CLI use. GitHub rejected PR creation, and the repository currently restricts it to collaborators. I understand that the contribution guide does not accept external code PRs, so I am sharing the root-cause analysis and reference implementation through the issue tracker instead. I respect the maintainers' decision on whether and how to use it.

items.body:
## Summary

Codex Desktop on Windows 10 becomes sluggish across all chats. Opening menus or Settings is especially slow. Restarting the app did not resolve it. During a captured Settings interaction, the desktop renderer had a CPU burst and the app-server request queue filled with `thread/attachment/list` calls during the same UI activity as a `thread/list` response.

## Environment

- Windows 10 Pro 22H2, build 19045, x64
- Codex Desktop Windows package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.924.2738.0` (verified from the running executable path)
- Desktop log build number: `11645`
- Local state: 3,182 total threads, 2,719 not archived
- Local `thread_attachments` table has 0 rows (this does not establish that no other attachment source exists)

## Reproduction

1. Open Codex Desktop with this existing local chat history.
2. Open a menu or Settings. The whole Codex UI is sluggish; the behavior affects all chats.
3. Restart Codex and repeat. The lag remains.

## Captured evidence

At 2026-09-28 16:12 Asia/Shanghai (08:12 UTC), while opening Settings:

- Main renderer CPU increased by 2.14 CPU-seconds during one wall-clock second. Its working set rose from about 632 MB to 722 MB.
- `thread/list` completed in 28 ms at 08:12:11.392 UTC.
- The surrounding burst logged `thread/attachment/list` for 100 distinct conversation IDs (166 log lines). The first queue rejections were logged at 08:12:11.373 UTC, **before** the `thread/list` response. These events coincide; the log does not prove that the list response caused the attachment requests.
- The app-server client queue reached 64 queued interactive requests with 4 in flight. 33 attachment-list requests were rejected with `App server request queue is full` (`-32001`).

A separate burst at about 08:11:26 UTC also covered 100 distinct conversation IDs and had 18 queue-full rejections. This indicates the fan-out is not specific to Settings. The exact UI trigger and source-code cause are not established.

During idle sampling after restart, the renderer used only 0.30 CPU-seconds across 6 seconds. System RAM and disk were not saturated. Thus the observed load is intermittent and coincides with request bursts, rather than constant CPU saturation.

The logs also show an unrelated-looking `git-init-watcher` retry every five seconds against a malformed path formed by joining two absolute Windows paths. Its relation to the UI lag is unproven.

## Expected behavior

Opening menus and Settings should remain responsive with a large local chat history. UI activity should not issue enough simultaneous per-thread attachment requests to exhaust the interactive request queue.

## Request

Please investigate which UI path issues attachment-list requests for this stable set of 100 threads, and whether they can be deduplicated, deferred until needed, or concurrency-limited. Please advise whether there is a supported user-side mitigation and which build contains a fix.

Related broader reports: #21211 (thread metadata/history performance), #20214 (Windows UI stutter). Those do not appear to document this exact 100-thread attachment-list burst and queue rejection.

No chat transcript, conversation ID, account detail, credential, full log, or personal filesystem path is included. Prepared with AI assistance at the user's request.

items.body:
## Feature request: Allow users to ask a question before approving or denying an action

### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex App / IDE Extension / CLI  
(Select whichever applies.)

### What feature would you like to see?

I would like Codex approval dialogs to include a third option in addition to **Approve** and **Deny**:

**Ask a question**

For example:

- Approve
- Ask a question
- Deny

When Codex requests permission to execute a command or perform another potentially sensitive action, I sometimes do not understand exactly what the requested action will do.

At that point, I do not want to approve it blindly, but I also do not want to deny it.

I would like to be able to ask Codex a question directly from the approval dialog before making the decision.

### Example workflow

Codex requests permission:

> Run: `sudo apt upgrade`

The approval dialog shows:

**Approve | Ask a question | Deny**

I select:

**Ask a question**

Then I can type:

> Could this affect the applications currently running on my server?

Codex explains the consequences, risks, and alternatives.

After answering, Codex should return to the original pending approval request:

**Approve | Ask another question | Deny**

### Why this would be useful

This would be especially useful for:

- developers working in unfamiliar parts of a system,
- less experienced developers,
- non-developers using Codex to build software,
- users working with servers, infrastructure, databases, or deployment tooling,
- security-sensitive commands,
- commands that modify files or system configuration.

Currently, an approval dialog can force the user into a binary decision even when the real problem is that they do not yet have enough information to make that decision.

The user should not have to choose between blindly approving an action and rejecting an otherwise valid action.

### Important distinction

This is not a request for Codex to automatically provide longer explanations before every approval.

The key feature is the ability for the **user to initiate a conversation while the approval is still pending**.

The approval request should remain open while the user asks one or more questions.

Conceptually:

```text
Codex wants to execute an action

[ Approve ]
[ Ask a question ]
[ Deny ]

        ↓

User asks:
"What exactly will this change?"

        ↓

Codex explains

        ↓

Original approval returns

[ Approve ]
[ Ask another question ]
[ Deny ]
```

### Possible UI

The approval dialog could contain:

**Approve**  
**Ask Codex**  
**Deny**

Alternatively, there could simply be a text input field below the approval request.

### Benefit

This would make approvals more genuinely human-in-the-loop.

Instead of approvals being only a security gate, they would become an informed decision point where the user can understand the action before granting permission.

~/.config/BraveSoftware/Brave-Origin/Default/Extensions/hehggadaopoacecdllhhajmbjkdcmajg

~/.local/bin/brave-browser -> /usr/bin/brave-origin

26.924.22138 (build 11645)

Unknown. This occurs during SSH bootstrap, before a model request; the remote host uses a custom OpenAI-compatible provider.

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm (macOS)

### What issue are you seeing?

The macOS Codex App repeatedly fails to connect to a Linux SSH host reached through a bastion. Interactive SSH, key authentication, the remote Codex CLI, and the managed remote app-server all work. The app instead reports "SSH connection failed" / "socket hang up" and retries.

The bastion silently drops non-interactive commands containing the literal agent-socket cleanup "rm -f", returning exit status 0 with empty stdout. The Codex App includes forwarded-SSH-agent socket cleanup in both its remote bootstrap and proxy paths even though this host has ForwardAgent no. The app can therefore receive a misleading successful bootstrap exit but fail to establish its WebSocket proxy.

Sanitized observations:

    ssh -T gated-remote 'printf READY'         # prints READY
    ssh -T gated-remote 'rm -f --version'       # exit 0, no output
    ssh -tt gated-remote                       # interactive shell works; typing rm -f --version prints its version
    ssh -T gated-remote 'codex app-server daemon start'  # succeeds

Invoking remote codex app-server proxy directly over the same SSH alias returns HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols; initialize, account/read, and model/list succeed. The installed standalone CLI is 0.157.1; its auto-updated managed app-server is 0.158.0.

Representative app log stages (host/account details removed):

    ssh_websocket_v0.remote_login_shell_command_completed operation=app_server_bootstrap code=0 stdout=""
    ssh_websocket_v0.proxy_command_starting operation=app_server_proxy
    app_server_connection.transport_connect_failed errorCode=ECONNRESET errorMessage="socket hang up"

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Configure a Linux SSH target through a bastion that permits ordinary non-interactive commands but silently filters a command containing the literal "rm -f" and returns exit status 0.
2. Define a concrete host alias for that target with ForwardAgent no. Confirm that interactive SSH and ordinary remote commands work; the harmless version query "rm -f --version" returns empty output only via non-interactive SSH.
3. Install/authenticate the remote Codex CLI and bootstrap a managed app-server. Confirm that remote app-server proxy completes a WebSocket upgrade over this same SSH alias.
4. Add or enable the alias in Codex App Settings > Connections. The app's bootstrap/proxy flow fails and the connection retries.

The result is the same when SSH ControlMaster multiplexing is disabled.

### What is the expected behavior?

For a connection with no forwarded SSH agent, avoid unnecessary forwarded-agent socket maintenance in remote bootstrap and proxy commands, or support attaching to an existing managed daemon using codex app-server daemon start and codex app-server proxy.

If a gateway silently drops a setup command while returning exit status 0, detect the missing expected result and report the failing stage instead of only "socket hang up" and repeated reconnects. This does not request bypassing the gateway's security policy.

### Additional information

Distinct from #36242 (SSH host discovery fails), #33879 (remote Codex missing from non-interactive PATH), and #24542 (unmanaged daemon respawn). This report concerns an unconditional forwarded-agent cleanup in the Desktop bootstrap/proxy path under a non-interactive command filter. items.body:
### What version of Codex is running?

codex-cli 0.157.1 (`codex --version`)

### What platform are you using?

Fedora CoreOS 44.20260829.3.1 (uCore)
Linux 7.1.10-200.fc44.x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux

### What issue are you seeing?

When Codex is run with `--yolo`, commands still execute with `NoNewPrivs: 1`. This prevents an otherwise valid passwordless sudo configuration from elevating privileges.

Inside the Codex command runner:

```text
$ awk '/^NoNewPrivs:/{print}' /proc/self/status
NoNewPrivs: 1

$ sudo -n true
sudo: The "no new privileges" flag is set, which prevents sudo from running as root.
If sudo is running in a container, you may need to adjust the container configuration to disable this.
```

The host is not configured with a kernel-wide prohibition against sudo. The same user can use sudo from the normal host terminal. The failure is specific to the Codex command environment.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start Codex with `--yolo` (or the equivalent full-access/dangerous mode).
2. Run `awk '/^NoNewPrivs:/{print}' /proc/self/status`.
3. Run `sudo -n true` or `sudo -n id`.
4. Observe that `NoNewPrivs` is `1` and sudo fails.

### Expected behavior

When the user explicitly selects `--yolo`/full host access, Codex should not impose or inherit `NoNewPrivs` for the command runner. Authorized sudo commands should behave as they do from the normal host terminal.

If the runner must retain `NoNewPrivs`, Codex should clearly report that sudo/root elevation is unavailable instead of presenting the session as full host access.

### Actual behavior

`--yolo` does not provide usable host-level execution for commands that require sudo. The runner retains `NoNewPrivs: 1`, and the restriction is irreversible for child processes.

### Additional diagnostics

```text
NoNewPrivs: 1
Seccomp: 2
```

This is not caused by the host's sudoers configuration or by a global kernel setting. Please clarify whether `--yolo` is intended to disable the outer command sandbox, and if so, why this process still inherits `NoNewPrivs`.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.154.0. `task_url()` is unchanged in rust-v0.158.0 (latest) and on current `main`.

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro

### Which model were you using?

N/A (not model-related)

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm (the URL is built client-side, so this is platform-independent)

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

N/A

### Codex doctor report

not available (the bug is in URL construction, independent of local install, config, or auth)

### What issue are you seeing?

`codex cloud exec` prints task links of the form `https://chatgpt.com/codex/tasks/<task_id>`. `codex cloud list` and the `url` field of `codex cloud list --json` return the same form.

Opening such a link in a browser signed in to the same ChatGPT account lands on `https://chatgpt.com/` (the ChatGPT home page) instead of the task. No error is shown; the task ID is silently dropped.

The same task opens at `https://chatgpt.com/codex/cloud/tasks/<task_id>`. That is also the `<link rel="canonical">` of the Codex task page. `https://chatgpt.com/remote/<task_id>` opens it as well.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Run `codex cloud exec --env <env_id> "<prompt>"`. It prints `https://chatgpt.com/codex/tasks/task_e_...`. You can also take `.tasks[].url` from `codex cloud list --json`.
2. Open that URL in a browser signed in to the same ChatGPT account.
3. The browser ends on `https://chatgpt.com/` and the task is not shown.
4. Replace `/codex/tasks/` with `/codex/cloud/tasks/`. The task page opens.

Reproduced on 2026-09-28 with 3 different task IDs, created on 2026-09-12 and 2026-09-28, in two separate browser profiles.

### What is the expected behavior?

Task links printed by `codex cloud` open the task.

### Additional information

**Web routing (observed in the browser on 2026-09-28)**

- A full page load of `/codex/tasks/<id>` is served by the main ChatGPT web app (route manifest `8aa0f368`), not by the Codex web app. That manifest has no `codex/tasks` route, so its catch-all `/*` route handles the request and navigates to `/`. The HTML response has the same length as the one for an arbitrary unknown path such as `/some/random/nonexistent/route`.
- `/codex/cloud/tasks/<id>` is served by the Codex web app (route manifest `80b15ad7`).
- The Codex web app still declares the legacy routes `routes/codex.tasks.$taskId._index` and `routes/codex.tasks._index`. Their loaders 307-redirect `/codex/...` to `/codex/cloud/...`, so the legacy URL seems intended to keep working. A direct load never reaches that app, though.
- A separate problem: client-side navigation to that legacy route inside the Codex app ends at `/codex/tasks/<id>/undefined/tasks/<id>` with "Application Error" (`No result found for routeId "routes/$"`). The redirect base constant appears to be uninitialized in the shipped chunk: its lazy-init function is exported, but the route module never calls it.

**CLI side**

`task_url()` in `codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/util.rs` hardcodes `/codex/tasks/` in all four branches, from rust-v0.154.0 through current `main`. Its result is the output of `codex cloud exec`, the output of `codex cloud list`, and the `url` field of `codex cloud list --json`.

**Possible fix**

There are two options:

- Restore the `/codex/tasks/*` → `/codex/cloud/tasks/*` redirect on the web side.
- Have the CLI emit the canonical path. The patch below does this.

The patch is also on a branch in my fork: https://github.com/limehee/codex/pull/1. That PR is a reference only and targets my fork's `main`, not this repository, per `docs/contributing.md`. With the pinned Rust 1.95.0 toolchain, `just test -p codex-cloud-tasks` passes (21/21). Against the old `task_url()`, the updated `format_task_list_lines_formats_urls` fails on exactly the two URL lines.

```diff
--- a/codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/util.rs
+++ b/codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/util.rs
@@ -137,15 +137,15 @@ pub async fn build_chatgpt_headers() -> HeaderMap {
 pub fn task_url(base_url: &str, task_id: &str) -> String {
     let normalized = normalize_base_url(base_url);
     if let Some(root) = normalized.strip_suffix("/backend-api") {
-        return format!("{root}/codex/tasks/{task_id}");
+        return format!("{root}/codex/cloud/tasks/{task_id}");
     }
     if let Some(root) = normalized.strip_suffix("/api/codex") {
-        return format!("{root}/codex/tasks/{task_id}");
+        return format!("{root}/codex/cloud/tasks/{task_id}");
     }
     if normalized.ends_with("/codex") {
-        return format!("{normalized}/tasks/{task_id}");
+        return format!("{normalized}/cloud/tasks/{task_id}");
     }
-    format!("{normalized}/codex/tasks/{task_id}")
+    format!("{normalized}/codex/cloud/tasks/{task_id}")
 }
--- a/codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/lib.rs
+++ b/codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/lib.rs
@@ -2332,12 +2332,12 @@ mod tests {
         assert_eq!(
             lines,
             vec![
-                "https://chatgpt.com/codex/tasks/task_1".to_string(),
+                "https://chatgpt.com/codex/cloud/tasks/task_1".to_string(),
                 "  [READY] Example task".to_string(),
                 "  Env  •  0s ago".to_string(),
                 "  +5/-2 • 3 files".to_string(),
                 String::new(),
-                "https://chatgpt.com/codex/tasks/task_2".to_string(),
+                "https://chatgpt.com/codex/cloud/tasks/task_2".to_string(),
                 "  [PENDING] No diff task".to_string(),
                 "  env-2  •  0s ago".to_string(),
                 "  no diff".to_string(),
```

`parse_task_id()` uses only the last path segment, so `/codex/tasks/<id>` URLs printed by earlier versions still parse.

**Not verified:** only one ChatGPT account was tested, so an account-scoped rollout can't be ruled out.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.924.2738.0 (also reproduced on 26.924.1866.0)

### What subscription do you have?

Pro

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

Archiving a thread that uses a Codex-managed worktree never completes when the Windows user profile folder name contains non-ASCII (Japanese) characters. The worktree snapshot step tries to create a directory whose path contains the user folder name with broken encoding, fails with EPERM, and the archive is retried endlessly.

Desktop log (user folder name replaced with `<garbled>`; in the real log it is mojibake of the Japanese name):

```
[worktree-snapshot] failed to snapshot worktree errorCode=EPERM errorMessage="EPERM: operation not permitted, mkdir 'C:\Users\<garbled>'"
[git] [worktree-delete] worker-failed errorCode=EPERM errorMessage="EPERM: operation not permitted, mkdir 'C:\Users\<garbled>'"
[managed-worktree-archive-queue] Worktree archive will be retried errorMessage="EPERM: operation not permitted, mkdir 'C:\Users\<garbled>'"
```

Impact:
- The worktree directory and its Git registration remain after archiving (the thread shows as archived).
- The retry loop writes 3,000+ log lines per day; the log folder has grown to about 133 MB.
- Managed worktrees keep accumulating under `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\worktrees` (69 so far).

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Use Windows with a user profile folder whose name contains Japanese characters (for example `C:\Users\<Japanese name>`).
2. In the Codex desktop app, start a thread in a Codex-managed worktree and make any change.
3. Archive the thread.
4. Check the desktop logs under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\OpenAI.Codex_2p2nqsd0c76g0\LocalCache\Local\Codex\Logs`: `worktree-snapshot` fails with `EPERM: operation not permitted, mkdir 'C:\Users\<garbled>'`, and `managed-worktree-archive-queue` keeps retrying.
5. The worktree folder under `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\worktrees` and its `git worktree list` entry remain.

Restarting or updating the app does not change the result.

### What is the expected behavior?

The worktree snapshot uses the correctly encoded (Unicode) user profile path, the archive completes, and the managed worktree is removed. If the snapshot fails, the retry should stop after a limit and the error should be shown in the app instead of retrying endlessly.

### Additional information

- Setting the user environment variable `HOME` to an ASCII path does not help, because this code path uses the Windows user profile folder, not `HOME`.
- Possibly related non-ASCII user path issues: #27543, #37740, #28691, #16918.

The user-authorized production map imagery update cannot continue through this browser route. Please identify why the navigation reached `error.taobao.com`, explain which restriction applies, and provide an approved way to restore this workflow if the block was unintended.
